title: When a Prediction Feeds Itself
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Mediterranean Travels
description: Label every link in three simplified prediction loops (predictive policing, student risk prediction, and a traffic forecast) as same or opposite direction, then classify each loop as reinforcing (self-fulfilling) or balancing (self-defeating).

educational.topic: Feedback loops in prediction systems: self-fulfilling and self-defeating predictions
learningObjectives: Differentiate reinforcing loops, in which a prediction helps bring itself about, from balancing loops, in which a prediction helps prevent itself, by labeling the direction of every link in three prediction loops and classifying each loop, with at least 9 of 10 links and all 3 loops correct.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Decompose-then-classify: the learner labels each causal link before classifying the loop, so the loop type is derived from its parts with the counting rule rather than guessed from the story
keyQuestions: If the first factor rises, does the second rise or fall?
How many opposite links does this loop contain, and is that number even or odd?
Does this prediction help bring itself about, or help prevent itself?
Which link would we change to weaken or reverse the loop?
commonMisconceptions: A loop with a minus sign in it must be balancing.
A prediction that comes true proves the model was accurate.
A forecast that failed was a bad forecast.
Taking more data from the same source fixes a feedback loop.
assessmentOpportunities: First-try scores on 10 links, 3 loops and 3 loop questions (mastery: links >= 9, loops = 3, questions >= 2).
Explain why a light road after a heavy-traffic forecast can mean the forecast worked.
